title: Reframing Accessibility
intro: Teams treat accessibility as a separate step — a compliance exercise tacked on at the end. Calabro's argument: accessibility is a proxy for good usability, and every accessibility failure is a usability failure for a much larger group.

learn.title: Every failure hits more people than you think
learn.text:
| Design flaw | Primary harm | Who else it hurts |
|---|---|---|
| Help hidden behind hover | Keyboard and touch users | Everyone who never finds it |
| Colour-only status indicators | Colour-blind users | Anyone in low light or on a poor display |
| Placeholder-only labels | Screen reader users | All users, as soon as they click in |

Treating the two as separate workstreams means solving the same problem twice.

try.q: A status is shown only by colour. Beyond colour-blind users, who else is affected?
options: Anyone on a poor display or in bright light
Only users who have disabled CSS
try.explain: Accessibility failures degrade the experience under ordinary real-world conditions.

learn.title: The review that changed the room
learn.text:
Consulting with a large organisation, Calabro reviewed a site the team felt good about: clean UI, generous white space, balanced typography.

Then they walked through the **top user tasks the way a real user would**. The vibe in the room shifted.

Important help content was hidden; key actions were unreachable without a mouse; status depended on colour alone.

try.q: What exposed the problems in his review?
options: Walking the top tasks as a real user would
Asking the team to rate their own work
try.explain: Looking at the page is not the same as using it.

learn.title: Usability under real-world conditions
learn.text:
The reframe: accessibility isn't a checklist that runs after design. It is what usability looks like when conditions aren't ideal — a user who is distracted, tired, on a phone in sunlight, or using a keyboard because their trackpad died.

So accessibility findings are usability findings, and belong in the same backlog with the same priority.

try.q: What does the article say accessibility is a proxy for?
try.explain: Which is why separate workstreams solve the same problem twice.

test.q: When do teams usually address accessibility?
options: At the end, as a compliance step
test.explain: The article argues against exactly that placement.

test.q: Why do placeholder-only labels hurt everyone?
options: The label vanishes as soon as you type
test.explain: It affects all users the moment they click in, not only assistive tech users.

test.q: What should happen to accessibility findings?
options: They go in the same backlog as usability findings
They go to a separate compliance team
They are scheduled after the release
They are logged against WCAG criteria only

test.q: What was the team's own assessment before the walkthrough?
options: They felt very good about how it looked
They had already run an audit
test.explain: Appearance and usability were being confused.

test.q: What is the cost of running accessibility as a separate workstream?
options: You solve the same problem twice
